proposals.name: Payload-per-word compression
proposals.instruction: Judge how much comic work each word does. Score 10 when the caption is at or near the shortest possible form that still delivers the joke -- a single word, a bare phrase, or a five-word line where deleting any word destroys it, and where no word is spent on setup, framing, or restating the drawing. Score 5 for a caption of ordinary conversational length in which roughly half the words are load-bearing. Score 0 for a caption that takes a long clause or two to arrive somewhere a much shorter line could have reached, or that pads the joke with framing words before and after it. Judge length only relative to the payload: a long caption in which every clause adds a distinct new turn is not penalized.
proposals.rationale: The slice separates extremely dense lines from diffuse ones with comparable content. R07 ('it's so ewe') and R23 ('wreckmaninoff') carry a full joke in one to three words; R50 ('he got indicted') and R05 ('you're rambling again') are similarly stripped. Against these, R31 ('remember when i was the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant') and R35 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') spend a long clause building toward a comparable payoff. A criterion bank that scores wit, relevance and cleverness separately can rate the long versions well on each while missing that the short ones are doing the same work at a fraction of the cost.

proposals.name: Pre-existing idiom literalized by the drawing
proposals.instruction: Score how far the caption's humor comes from an idiom, proverb, or fixed phrase that already exists in English and whose literal reading happens to be exactly what is drawn. Score 10 when the caption is (near) verbatim a phrase people already say, and the drawing makes its literal sense true, so the joke feels discovered rather than constructed. Score 5 when a familiar phrase is present but has been reworded enough that the recognition is muted, or when the literal reading only loosely matches the drawing. Score 0 when the caption is a bespoke sentence with no fixed-phrase substrate, or quotes a familiar phrase whose literal meaning has nothing to do with the picture.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') and R46 ('you need to get your act together') are untouched idioms that the drawing renders literally true -- a wolf buying wool, a circus act in the living room. R12 ('detect irony') and R44 ('gravity of our situation') work the same way. Contrast R30 ('i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout') and R09 ('let's do the saturn ring toss'), which are invented sentences with no found-phrase collision. Rubric criteria about wordplay or cleverness treat constructed puns and found idioms alike, so this axis is invisible to them.

proposals.name: Dual-anchor pun: specific object plus idiom
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption's pivot word is anchored simultaneously to a specific object or particular in the drawing AND to an independent idiomatic or figurative sense, so that both readings are fully true at once. Score 10 when both anchors are precise: the literal sense names something concretely present in the picture (not merely its general category), and the figurative sense is a complete, natural expression. Score 5 when one anchor is solid and the other is approximate or forced. Score 0 when the pun only touches one sense, only touches the broad category of the scene, or requires the reader to grant an inexact word to make it work.
proposals.rationale: R01/R49 ('no quarter will be given') lock the coin-operated ride's literal quarter to the military phrase and to the child's historical-general costume at the same time. R56 ('88 keys and no locks') binds the exact number of piano keys to house keys and locks. Compare R24 ('the only house i could find under a grand'), which reaches the piano's name but leaves the crash, the damage and the speaker unaccounted for, and R55 ('that's a blues jay'), whose pun touches only the bird and not the guitar, hat or microphone. A generic 'contains wordplay' criterion cannot separate a two-anchor lock from a one-anchor near-miss.

proposals.name: Restates what is already visible
proposals.instruction: Score the caption on NOT narrating the drawing. Score 10 when the caption adds information, a stance, or a frame that is nowhere in the picture, so that reading it changes what the picture means. Score 5 when it partly points at visible content but still contributes an angle. Score 0 when the caption's main content is a paraphrase of what the reader can already see -- naming the anomaly, describing what the characters are doing, or stating the obvious explanation for the scene -- so that removing the caption would lose almost nothing.
proposals.rationale: R20 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too') states the drawing's whole premise back to the reader; R13 ('honey, the remote is in your hand') and R16 ('i see you ate some of dad's favorite ice cream') supply the literal explanation the scene already implies. R43 and R57 both spell out that the bear used to catch fish, which the drawing's incongruity has already established. Scorecard criteria for relevance or fit reward exactly this tight coupling to the image, so premise-restatement scores HIGH on relevance while being the least informative thing a caption can do.

proposals.name: Implies an off-panel history or consequence
proposals.instruction: Score how much unseen world the caption creates. Score 10 when the line forces the reader to infer a specific event, relationship, or prior state that is not drawn -- a number, an accusation, a loss, a recent history -- so that the single panel becomes the last frame of a longer story. Score 5 when a vague elsewhere is gestured at without specifics. Score 0 when the caption stays entirely inside the moment depicted and implies no before, after, or elsewhere.
proposals.rationale: R54 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning') implies an off-panel massacre that the placid drawing conceals; R48 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') implies a whole marital history behind an indoor metal-detector search; R37 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') and R32 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') both plant precise off-panel events. Against these, R30 and R14 ('guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first') stay wholly inside the depicted second. Rubrics rarely ask whether a caption manufactures a world, only whether it fits the one shown.

proposals.name: Speaker identity is itself the reveal
proposals.instruction: Score whether working out who is speaking is part of the joke. Score 10 when the caption is only fully funny once the reader assigns it to a specific, non-default speaker in the scene -- often the animal, the object, the intruder, or the character least expected to talk -- and that assignment is unambiguous but not immediate. Score 5 when the speaker is a plausible non-default character but identifying them adds little. Score 0 when the line could be said by any character, or is said by the obvious default speaker, so that attribution contributes nothing.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('all my evaluation said was good girl') only resolves once the reader realizes the speaker is a dog talking about a performance review; R25 ('you should see the breasts') and R34 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night') both depend on the reader placing the line in a specific mouth. By contrast, R41 ('it took him six days to make') and R47 ('what are we, neanderthals') are said by the obvious character with no attributional work. A bank that scores 'consistent with the characters' rewards the safe default assignment and cannot see the extra beat.

proposals.name: Dark content delivered in a placid register
proposals.instruction: Score the gap between the severity of what the caption says and the calm of how it says it. Score 10 when genuinely grim, morbid, cruel, or transgressive content is delivered in flat administrative, domestic, or conversational language, with no signalling word (no 'unfortunately', 'sadly', 'oh god') to mark it as dark. Score 5 when dark content is present but the delivery flags it as dark. Score 0 when there is no dark content, or when the darkness is stated so plainly and expectedly that no tonal gap exists.
proposals.rationale: R42 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent') puts an ugly proposition in cocktail-party debate register; R54, R37 and R34 all report grim facts in ordinary domestic phrasing. Compare R14 ('guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first'), which acknowledges mortality in the tone mortality invites, and R53 ('on the plus side, mass extinction is a really cool band name'), which explicitly flags its own silver lining. Criteria for tone-appropriateness or good taste will penalize the first group and credit the second, which is the wrong direction on this slice.

proposals.name: Topical transposition that reframes the whole scene
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption maps the entire drawn scene onto a contemporary public or civic situation, such that every element of the picture acquires a second reading. Score 10 when one short line relocates the whole tableau -- all the figures, not one of them -- into a recognizable current-affairs frame that the reader completes unaided. Score 5 when a topical reference is present but only recolors part of the scene, or is bolted on. Score 0 when there is no topical dimension, or when the topical reference is stale, name-dropped without a mapping, or requires the caption to explain itself.
proposals.rationale: R29 ('they're still looking for votes') converts an indoor metal-detector search into an election dispute in five words, and R59 ('it's from our new white house collection') turns a wolf-in-sheep's-clothing rack into a political joke. R39, R45 and R50 do the same to a circus parade. Contrast R21 ('six feet dude. six. feet'), a topical reference dropped onto a desert-island scene it does not reorganize, and R31, which needs a long clause to set its topicality up. Scorecards that credit 'reference' or 'cleverness' per se cannot distinguish a whole-scene remapping from a bolted-on allusion.

proposals.name: Reliance on a stock joke template
proposals.instruction: Score freedom from recognizable joke scaffolds. Score 10 when the caption's construction is not traceable to a familiar joke shape and the reader could not have guessed its form from the drawing. Score 5 when a familiar shape is used but bent noticeably. Score 0 when the caption fills in a well-worn template -- 'does this make me look X', 'when I was a kid we had to Y', 'enough about me, what about you', 'what are we, Z?', 'I'm thinking takeout' -- with the scene's nouns substituted in, so a competent writer would have produced it as a first attempt.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big') is the 'does this make me look fat' template with the wolf's nouns dropped in; R26 ('enough about me. you're an accountant?'), R57 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish'), R30 and R47 are each an off-the-shelf frame filled from the picture. Because these templates are grammatical, on-topic and clearly a joke, criteria for coherence, relevance and humor-presence all pass them, which is precisely how a scorecard over-credits the most predictable entry in the pool.

proposals.name: Obliquity of the mundane concern under a normalized absurdity
proposals.instruction: Given that the caption treats the impossible element as unremarkable, score how non-obvious the mundane thing the speaker cares about instead is. Score 10 when the substituted concern is one the reader would never have predicted from the scene, yet is instantly recognizable as a real human preoccupation once said. Score 5 when the concern is the second or third thing one might guess. Score 0 when the caption normalizes the absurdity but then worries about the single most predictable adjacent thing -- the logistics, the rules, or the literal mechanics of the impossible element itself.
proposals.rationale: R46 ('you need to get your act together'), R12 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony') and R44 ('of course we understand the gravity of our situation') accept the absurdity and pivot to a concern nobody would have guessed. R38 ('actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets') and R09 ('let's do the saturn ring toss') also normalize, but land on the first-guess concern: the building's pet rules, the next party game. The normalization move alone is easy to score and easy to credit; its obliquity is the part that separates this slice.

proposals.name: Non-dialogue label or verdict form that lands
proposals.instruction: Score captions that are not spoken dialogue -- a title, a noun phrase, a coinage, a one-word verdict -- on whether the non-dialogue form is itself doing comic work. Score 10 when the caption is a label or bare fragment and that framing is exactly why it works: it names the scene from outside with a finality no line of dialogue could achieve. Score 5 when it is a fragment that would have worked equally well as dialogue. Score 0 when it is a fragment merely because it is incomplete or elliptical, leaving the reader to supply the missing joke. Captions that are ordinary complete dialogue should be scored 0 on this axis without prejudice; this criterion measures only whether a departure from dialogue is earned.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('wreckmaninoff') and R45 ('republican primary ticket') are titles, not speech, and the deadpan naming is the whole joke; R50 ('he got indicted') is a bare verdict. This is a shape that a criterion bank built around speech will penalize or fail to see -- checks for natural dialogue, speaker plausibility, or complete-sentence quality all read these as defective, even though the caption form in this contest permits a title.

proposals.name: Sound-pun aimed at the scene's central absurdity
proposals.instruction: For captions whose humor is phonetic (a homophone, near-homophone, portmanteau, or respelling), score whether the transformed word names the thing that makes the drawing strange, rather than an incidental detail. Score 10 when the sound-play lands squarely on the central incongruity, so the pun and the premise are the same object. Score 5 when it lands on a real element of the scene that is not the source of the strangeness. Score 0 when the phonetic play is on a peripheral or merely adjacent detail, or when it is a sound joke with no anchor in the picture at all. Captions with no phonetic play should be scored 0 on this axis without prejudice.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('it's so ewe') puts the pun exactly on the sheep-disguise premise, and R23 ('wreckmaninoff') fuses the wreck and the piano into one word. R55 ('that's a blues jay') and R52 ('a hole-in-the-wall place you'll love') are competent phonetic puns aimed at the bird's species and the mouse's habitat -- true details, but not the source of the incongruity, which is the guitar and the lab coat respectively. A bank that scores 'contains a pun' or 'wordplay quality' will rate all four similarly.

proposals.name: Verbal throat-clearing before the joke
proposals.instruction: Score the absence of scaffolding phrases that announce, cushion, or introduce the punchline. Score 10 when the caption begins in the joke, with no lead-in. Score 0 when it opens with or leans on discourse framing -- 'believe it or not', 'actually', 'guess i'll', 'i don't know about you, but', 'on the plus side', 'i can usually X, but', 'remember when' -- that tells the reader a joke is arriving instead of delivering it. Score 5 for a single light connective that also carries meaning. Judge only the framing words, not the caption's total length.
proposals.rationale: R20 opens 'believe it or not', R38 opens 'actually', R14 opens 'guess i'll', R30 opens 'i don't know about you, but', R53 opens 'on the plus side', R35 opens 'i can usually... but' -- six captions in this slice that spend their opening on announcing the joke. The tightest lines in the slice (R07, R23, R29, R05) have none. Scaffolding makes a caption read as fluent, well-formed prose, which is exactly what fluency- or naturalness-shaped criteria reward.

proposals.name: Second beat that sends the reader back to the drawing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption has a delayed payoff requiring a return to the picture. Score 10 when the caption reads one way on first pass and a second, funnier meaning arrives only after the reader re-checks a specific element of the drawing -- and both readings remain valid. Score 5 when there is a mild delay but the second reading adds little. Score 0 when the entire meaning is delivered on first pass with nothing held back, or when the delayed reading, once found, is not funnier than the first.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('it's slow now, but we'll be pooped by the end of the night') reads as ordinary shift-talk until the reader re-registers that the 'tunnel' is a digestive tract; R25 ('you should see the breasts') sends you back to the grill to scale up an unseen bird; R01 does the same with the ride's coin slot. Compare R10 ('three more dollars and we can order a pizza') and R27, which are fully unpacked on the first pass. Criteria that score clarity or immediate comprehensibility actively penalize the delayed-payoff structure.

proposals.name: Cultural callback transformed, not merely cited
proposals.instruction: For captions invoking a song, story, character, or well-known text, score whether the borrowed material has been put to work. Score 10 when the reference is bent so that its original words acquire a new and situation-specific meaning in the drawing -- the reader gets both the recognition and a fresh joke. Score 5 when the reference is apt and pleasantly placed but its meaning is unchanged by the scene. Score 0 when the caption merely names or lists the reference's contents and relies on recognition alone for its effect. Captions with no cultural callback should be scored 0 on this axis without prejudice.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('don't think of them as discouraging words so much as constructive criticism') takes a line from a familiar song and reinterprets it as workplace feedback; R22 and R33 turn a children's round into a grave prognosis; R11 ('we have never had a cross word between us') bends the Holmes register onto a crossword. Against these, R18 ('would you rather get back your truck, your dog, or your wife') and R53 ('mass extinction is a really cool band name') deliver recognition with no transformation. A bank scoring 'clever reference' or 'cultural literacy' will credit citation and transformation identically.

proposals.name: Word count and clause-scaffold verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual bulk in the caption only. Count the words and the number of independent or subordinate clauses, and add weight for scaffolding material that lengthens the line without adding a new referent: introductory adverbials, hedges ('i think', 'i don't know about you, but'), relative clauses, coordinated second sentences, and appositive asides. 0 = a single word or a bare noun phrase; 5 = one ordinary sentence of roughly eight to twelve words; 10 = two or more full sentences, or one sentence of twenty-plus words with several clauses. Judge LENGTH AND CLAUSE STRUCTURE ONLY. Do NOT judge whether the caption is funny, apt, well-paced, or good for the cartoon; a long caption and a short caption can both be excellent, and you are not assessing that.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1. Raw token bulk tracks the split in this slice almost monotonically and independently of aptness. R23 ('you're rambling again', three words) and R38 ('wreckmaninoff', one word) sit at dense_pct .991 and .794 with card_pct .474 and .164, while R46 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') and R17 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make') are the two longest lines in the slice at dense_pct .006 and .028 against card_pct .735 and .847. R13 and R27 repeat the pattern. Length is a formatting property of the submission, not a property of how well the line answers its drawing, and a rubric that rewards elaborated criteria will absorb it mechanically; it must be discounted rather than banked.

proposals.name: Transcription and typography conventions in the entry line
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption carries marked transcription or typographic apparatus, relative to a bare lowercase unpunctuated line. Add extent for each of: internal quotation marks around reported speech; a terminal period, question mark or exclamation point; double-hyphen or em-dash breaks; ellipses; apostrophe elision of a final g or other dialect spelling; the caption being split into two or more sentences by mid-line periods; digits written as numerals rather than words; any capitalisation at all. 0 = plain lowercase, single clause, no terminal mark; 10 = several of these devices at once. Judge ONLY the presence and density of these orthographic marks. Do NOT judge whether the punctuation is correct, tasteful, or well used, and do NOT judge the joke.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 (transcription conventions). The corpus is mostly case-folded and unpunctuated, so the residual marks are compilation and typing artefacts rather than authorial craft, yet they are strongly text-visible and hence learnable. R40 carries both internal single quotes and a terminal period ('all my evaluation said was \'good girl.\''), R29 carries a bare double-hyphen ('no bag--my cubs...'), R19 is split into three orthographic units by mid-line periods ('six feet dude. six. feet'), and R48 uses dialect elision ('comin\'') where its near-twin R42 uses the full 'coming'. R42 and R48 are the same joke and differ chiefly in this apparatus, which makes it a clean nuisance axis: nothing about who typed the apostrophe bears on whether the line is a good entry for the drawing.
proposals.upstream_parent: transcription and compilation conventions applied by whoever prepared the entry list (and the entrant's own typing habits)

proposals.name: Item lacks usable cartoon context; caption reads free-standing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item, as presented, gives no drawing to read the caption against, so that the caption must be interpreted as a free-standing line. Score 10 when the cartoon field is absent, empty, or a placeholder such as '[no description available]'. Score high (7-9) when a description is present but so short or generic that it names no object, action or character the caption could hook onto. Score low (0-2) when the description names specific figures, props and the visual incongruity. Judge ONLY how much drawing-side information the item supplies. Do NOT judge whether the caption is good, and do NOT try to imagine what the missing drawing might have been.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. (a) An unseen factor beyond the caption text is whether the description generator succeeded for that cartoon. (b) Its textual fingerprint is fully visible: the '[no description available]' placeholder in the item record. (c) A judge can score the placeholder without any conjecture. Seven rows in the slice carry it and they cluster hard on one side: R08, R22, R23, R40, R42 and R48 are all dense_high_card_low (dense_pct .802, .773, .991, .827, .951, .947 against card_pct .248, .234, .474, .200, .444, .191), with only R58 on the other side. A criterion-scored rubric that must ask 'does this fit the drawing' is structurally starved on these rows while an end-to-end reader is not, so the placeholder predicts the disagreement directly. It is an artefact of corpus preparation and carries no information about entry quality; it must never be bankable.
proposals.upstream_parent: corpus assembly and the automatic description pipeline (which items got a description generated)

proposals.name: Unanchored deixis: opening pronoun or demonstrative with no in-text antecedent
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption's referents are left to the picture rather than named in the words. Add extent for: a bare pronoun or demonstrative in the first three words with no antecedent inside the caption ('it's', 'they're', 'he', 'them', 'that'); definite noun phrases introduced with 'the' as if already known; and an overall proportion of unnamed to named participants. Subtract extent when the caption names its own subject, situation or props explicitly enough to be understood with the drawing removed. 0 = fully self-contained; 10 = the line is uninterpretable without the picture. Judge ONLY referential self-containment. Do NOT judge whether depending on the picture is a virtue or a fault here, and do NOT judge the humour.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. (a) The unseen factor is how the entrant composed: staring at the drawing and letting it carry the nouns, versus assembling a transportable joke. (b) The fingerprint is pronoun-first, antecedent-free syntax. (c) That is scorable from the words alone. R05 ('they're still looking for votes', dense_pct .970 / card_pct .085), R32 ('he got indicted', .957 / .282) and R01 ('it's from our new white house collection', .940 / .187) all open on a referent that exists only in the drawing and all sit at the dense-high, card-low extreme; contrast R33 and R34, which name their own situation ('i'm thinking takeout', 'when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish') and sit card-high. A criterion bank that asks about clarity or standalone readability penalises exactly this syntax. Tagged mixed because image-grounded composition plausibly also produces genuinely better entries, so the discount should be reported as a band.
proposals.upstream_parent: image-grounded composition (the entrant writing while looking at the drawing, versus writing a portable line)

proposals.name: Partisan-political and news-event subject matter
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption's subject matter is drawn from electoral politics, government, or a specific news event, as opposed to domestic, natural-world, workplace or interpersonal material. Count references to parties, candidacies, primaries, slates, tickets, votes and ballots, indictments, trials, officials, government buildings and administrations, and any phrasing that reads as commentary on a public controversy. 0 = no political or news content at all; 10 = the whole caption is a political reference and nothing else. Judge ONLY the topic. Do NOT judge whether the political joke is sharp, fair, dated or apt, and do NOT judge whether such content suits the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 (news cycle) with MODE 2 structure: the unseen factor is what was in the news that week, and its fingerprint is the political vocabulary itself. The channel is nearly deterministic on one side of this slice: R05 ('they're still looking for votes'), R16 ('it's the republican slate of candidates'), R25 ('republican primary ticket'), R32 ('he got indicted') and R01 ('our new white house collection') are all dense_high_card_low, with card_pct between .085 and .282 and dense_pct between .751 and .970. Topic is not craft: the same drawing supports an equally good non-political line, and the criterion bank evidently has no place to credit topicality. Tagged mixed because a reference that was live that week can genuinely land for contemporaneous readers, so political content is not purely nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the news cycle live at the moment of that week's contest

proposals.name: Era-locked idiom dating the entry to a period of the series
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption's vocabulary and references place it in a particular stretch of years rather than being period-neutral. Add extent for: pandemic-era public-health idiom (distancing measured in feet, shutdowns, immunity language, masking, remote work); named consumer technologies and platforms; slang or catchphrases whose currency is confined to a decade; and references to institutions or practices that have since changed. 0 = the wording would read the same in any decade; 10 = the line could be dated to within a couple of years from vocabulary alone. Judge ONLY period-specificity of the wording. Do NOT judge whether the reference is stale, timely, clever or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 (position in container). The date is unobservable, but era leaves a lexical trace, and the trace splits this slice on both sides, which is exactly what a nuisance channel looks like. R19 ('six feet dude. six. feet', dense_pct .040 / card_pct .953) and R15 ('the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant', .142 / .781) are pandemic-dated and card-high; R24 ('they claim they have herd immunity', .563 / .047) is pandemic-dated and card-low; R03 ('no tv or iphone', .253 / .845) is dated by a product name. Because the same era-marking can push either model, it is predictive without being quality: when an entry was written is not a property of how well it serves its drawing. Distinct from B05, which scores topic rather than the datedness of the wording.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the contest within the long-running series (which era's conventions and idiom the entry comes from)

proposals.name: First-thought pun on the drawing's most salient word
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption is built on the single most obvious lexical hook the drawing offers: a homophone, near-homophone, portmanteau, or dead idiom keyed to the one word an ordinary viewer would name first when describing the picture (for a sheep drawing, wool or ewe; for a piano, keys or grand; for a crossword, cross word). Score 10 when the whole caption is that one pivot and nothing else; score 5 when the obvious hook is present but embedded in other material; score 0 when the caption reaches an angle that does not turn on the picture's headline noun. Judge ONLY how directly the caption lands on the picture's most available wordplay. Do NOT judge whether the pun is groanworthy or delightful, and do NOT judge execution.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 (position in the entry stream). The entry count is unobservable, but convergence leaves a fingerprint: the consensus angle is the drawing's headline noun. The slice is full of it and it splits the two models. R28 ('it's so ewe', dense_pct .981 / card_pct .159), R52 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes', .876 / .174), R07 ('i love that it's 100 wool', .949 / .301) and R38 ('wreckmaninoff', .794 / .164) are card-low; R21 ('the only house i could find under a grand', .047 / .607) and R43 ('that's a blues jay', .148 / .779) are card-high. How crowded an angle is says nothing about whether this instance of it is a good entry, so it must be discounted, not banked. Tagged mixed because a strongly invited pun is often also genuinely apt.
proposals.upstream_parent: position within the flood of entries for that cartoon (how many other entrants reached the same angle)

proposals.name: Caption narrates or explains the drawing's incongruity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption states, describes or accounts for what is visibly odd in the picture, rather than speaking from inside the situation as though it were unremarkable. Add extent for: naming the anomalous element outright; a line whose content is an observation about the anomaly; explanatory framing that tells the reader how to read the image ('believe it or not', 'actually', 'no, that's a'); and any restatement of a fact the drawing already shows. Score 0 when the caption presupposes the whole situation and adds a remark that only makes sense if the oddity is taken for granted. Judge ONLY how much of the drawing the words re-tell. Do NOT judge whether explaining is a weakness, and do NOT judge the humour.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 and MODE 4 (entrant's practice). (a) The unseen factor is how many contests the entrant has worked; (b) its fingerprint is precisely the explain-versus-presuppose choice, which is visible in the words; (c) a judge scores the retelling, never the conjectured entrant. R37 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too', dense_pct .087 / card_pct .626) and R09 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big', .214 / .822) both spell out the visual joke and are card-high; R36 ('actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets', .415 / .902) uses the explanatory 'actually'. Against these, R59 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning', .880 / .161) and R49 ('no. no quarter will be given', .945 / .302) presuppose everything. Tagged mixed and honestly so: practice plausibly causes better entries as well as this fingerprint, so the discounted and undiscounted readouts should both be shown.
proposals.upstream_parent: the entrant's practice in this format (a serial entrant's internalised refusal to explain the drawing, versus a one-off submitter)

proposals.name: Generic caption-shaped joke: scaffolded setup with tidy payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption takes the safe, recognisably caption-shaped form that a competent writer with no knowledge of this particular contest would produce. Add extent for: a discourse-marker opener ('i don't know about you, but', 'on the plus side', 'believe it or not', 'when i was a kid', 'no, that's'); a comma-separated setup-then-payoff structure; a complete, grammatical, self-explaining sentence that resolves its own joke inside the line; a conversational speech-act frame (correction, reminiscence, reassurance, suggestion) laid over the picture; and an ending that ties the observation off rather than leaving it open. 0 = the line has no such scaffolding and does not resolve itself; 10 = every element of the standard shape is present. Judge ONLY the presence of this conventional form. Do NOT judge whether the caption is well written or funny; well-formedness is what you are measuring, not merit.
proposals.rationale: MODE 5 (required). This is the fingerprint of the line a general model would nominate, and it loads almost entirely on the card-high, dense-low half. R33 ('i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout', dense_pct .155 / card_pct .975), R56 ('on the plus side, mass extinction is a really cool band name', .021 / .516), R37 ('believe it or not, ...', .087 / .626), R34 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish', .452 / .968) and R13 ('enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting', .065 / .877) all take the standard shape. A bank of explicitly written criteria is close to a rendering of that generic prior, so it scores form; the editors' actual taste and this prior come apart, which is exactly why the form must be a declared nuisance. Tagged mixed because well-formedness weakly co-occurs with real competence.
proposals.upstream_parent: generic competent-writer / general-purpose language-model prior over what a caption should look like

proposals.name: Content outside the venue's printed register (bodily, sexual, injury, transgressive)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption's content sits outside the restrained register a general-audience magazine cartoon caption normally occupies. Add extent for: sexual or anatomical reference and double entendre; scatological or excretory wording; bodily injury, mutilation or death treated as the joke's material; language about consent, coercion or violence; and any wording whose bluntness would need an editor's second look. 0 = wholly mild and printable without comment; 10 = the caption's entire payload is transgressive material. Judge ONLY how far the content sits from the mild register. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is funny, offensive, tasteful or warranted; you are measuring distance from the house register, not approving or condemning it.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 (house style) with MODE 2 structure: the unseen factor is a venue-level publication norm, and its fingerprint is the lexical register of the line. Every clearly off-register row in the slice lands dense-high and card-low: R41 ('you should see the breasts', dense_pct .929 / card_pct .042), R44 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night', .741 / .040), R26 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent', .859 / .134) and R14 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg', .656 / .076) — the four lowest card percentiles among dense-high items. A written criterion bank encodes decorum explicitly and an end-to-end reader does not, so register alone drives the gap. Whether a line is printable in a given venue is a property of the venue, not of how well the words answer that drawing, so it is a pure nuisance and must never be bankable.
proposals.upstream_parent: house style and editorial register of the magazine running the contest (the kind of joke it prints and the kind it never prints)

proposals.name: Idiom/cliché literalized onto a specific visual detail
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the caption takes a common idiom, cliché, or fixed phrase and re-grounds it literally in a specific visual particular of the cartoon (not just the general topic). 10 = a well-known idiom is mapped onto an exact, non-obvious visual detail so the phrase now reads as literally true in-scene; 5 = an idiom is present but connects only loosely/generically to the scene; 0 = no idiom or fixed phrase is being literalized at all.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('i will give you no quarter') and R40 ('no. no quarter will be given') literalize the idiom 'give no quarter' onto the coin-operated horse ride's literal quarter-coin mechanism; R36 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') literalizes the idiom onto the wolf's wool costume; R22 ('they claim they have herd immunity') literalizes 'herd immunity' onto the sheep/dog resemblance. All three are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the scorecard undercredits this device.

proposals.name: Layered/compound wordplay stacking multiple puns
proposals.instruction: Score how many independent puns, double meanings, or wordplay devices are stacked within the single caption so they mutually reinforce one joke. 10 = two or more distinct wordplay mechanisms compound in one short line; 5 = exactly one clean pun with no stacking; 0 = no wordplay present.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('wreckmaninoff') fuses 'wreck' with the composer Rachmaninoff, simultaneously invoking the piano, the destruction, and classical-music snobbery in one coined word; R46 ('now the house has 88 keys and no locks') stacks the piano-keys pun with a literal 'keys and locks' security pun. Both are dense_high_card_low (dense .794/.714 vs card .164/.117), suggesting the scorecard undercredits compounded wordplay relative to simpler entries.

proposals.name: Specific topical/political reference fused to the scene
proposals.instruction: Score how specifically the caption imports a real-world, current-events, or political reference and fuses it to the depicted absurdity, rather than staying generic. 10 = a precise, timely, real-world reference (a named institution, a live political controversy, a legal event) is seamlessly mapped onto the cartoon's logic; 5 = a vague or generic 'real life' gesture with no specific reference; 0 = no topical/political content at all.
proposals.rationale: R39 ('they're still looking for votes') maps metal-detector search behavior onto election-fraud discourse; R51/R57 ('republican primary ticket' / 'it's the republican slate of candidates') map a circus-animal parade onto electoral politics; R31 ('it's from our new white house collection') maps a wolf-in-sheep's-clothing costume onto political messaging; R04 ('he got indicted') does the same for the same cartoon. All are dense_high_card_low with especially depressed card_pct (.030-.395), suggesting the scorecard bank underweights topical satire.

proposals.name: Meta-humor about the joke/genre itself
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption comments on the act of joke-telling, the contest genre, or the comedic convention of noticing absurdity, rather than staying purely inside the depicted scene. 10 = the caption knowingly winks at its own status as a joke or at the reader's/judge's expectations; 5 = a mild self-aware aside; 0 = the caption is entirely diegetic with no self-reference.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony') turns the cartoon's metal-detector search into a comment on the caption's own ironic mode; R01 ('you're rambling again') reads as commentary on rambling/verbosity itself, functioning independent of any specific cartoon content. Both are dense_high_card_low (dense .859/.991 vs card .353/.474).

proposals.name: Borrowed song/fixed-phrase register clashing with scene
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the caption repurposes a recognizable song lyric or culturally fixed phrase, importing that source's original emotional register (nostalgic, cheerful, innocent) into a starkly mismatched context for ironic effect. 10 = source text is clearly recognizable and its imported tone strongly clashes with the caption's new (e.g., bleak or clinical) context; 0 = no borrowed cultural text is present.
proposals.rationale: R15 ('it's time to accept that she's never coming round the mountain') and R37 ('i think we need to face the possibility that she won't be comin' round the mountain') both repurpose the cheerful folk song 'She'll Be Comin' Round the Mountain' as somber, resigned language about loss. Both are dense_high_card_low (dense .951/.947 vs card .444/.191), and the pattern repeats across two independently-submitted captions for what appears to be the same cartoon, suggesting robustness.

proposals.name: Deadpan institutional/bureaucratic register vs. absurd scene
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the caption speaks in flat, procedural, clinical, or officious diction about a wildly fantastical event, producing humor purely from the mismatch between voice and content. 10 = sustained formal/bureaucratic phrasing applied to an outlandish scene with no acknowledgment of its strangeness; 0 = the caption's diction matches the scene's fantastical register (excited, informal, or matter-of-fact about the fantasy).
proposals.rationale: R08 ('well of course we understand the gravity of our situation') uses formal, almost committee-speak phrasing about lunching beside the Grim Reaper; R50 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') mimics workplace safety-record language for the same scene. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .824/.741 vs card .289/.195).

proposals.name: Purposeful edgy/taboo content (sexual, dark, or transgressive)
proposals.instruction: Score how effectively the caption uses taboo, sexual, or transgressive content as a deliberate comic device rather than gratuitously. 10 = subversive or risqué content lands as a sharp, purpose-built joke tightly tied to the scene; 5 = mild edginess with unclear payoff; 0 = caption is entirely safe/anodyne with no risk taken.
proposals.rationale: R26 ('you should see the breasts') uses a crude double entendre (turkey/meat breast vs. human anatomy) on the oversized-meat cartoon; R23 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent') imports a charged social debate into a giant-mosquito small-talk scene. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .929/.859 vs card .042/.134), the two lowest card scores in the whole slice, suggesting the scorecard bank may actively penalize or fail to credit transgressive material that the dense model rewards.

proposals.name: Late-caption reveal that recontextualizes the whole line
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption withholds its point until the final word(s), forcing a re-reading of everything preceding it once the payoff lands. 10 = a strong late pivot that recasts the entire preceding clause in a new light; 0 = the caption states its point immediately with no structural delay or reversal.
proposals.rationale: R48 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') builds a neutral question that only reveals its accusatory sting on the final clause; R39 ('they're still looking for votes') reframes an innocuous couch scene only once 'votes' recontextualizes the search as electoral. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .836/.970 vs card .338/.085).

proposals.name: Plausible, single-mechanism, in-character naturalism
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption reads as something a real person would plausibly and simply say in that moment, resolving the scene's oddity with one clean, low-complexity, common-sense explanation and no wordplay. 10 = caption is a completely natural, single-idea line a person would actually utter, with the absurdity treated matter-of-factly; 0 = caption is abstract, referential, or built entirely on wordplay rather than a plausible spoken line.
proposals.rationale: R12 ('i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout') and R13 ('i see you ate some of dad's favorite ice cream') both read as ordinary, single-idea spoken lines that simply narrate a mundane explanation for the heavily-secured kitchen. Both are dense_low_card_high (dense .155/.259 vs card .975/.885), suggesting this plain naturalism is exactly what the scorecard is rewarding that the dense model discounts.

proposals.name: Self-contained wit independent of cartoon-specific detail
proposals.instruction: Score how well the caption's humor works as free-standing text even without knowledge of the specific cartoon's visual details. 10 = the line is a complete, funny or pointed utterance on its own, with no dependence on any particular visual element; 0 = the joke is unintelligible or meaningless without the exact visual detail it references.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('you're rambling again') and R18 ('don't think of them as discouraging words so much as constructive criticism') both land as complete character-voice lines that require no specific visual anchor to be legible, and both are drawn from rows where no cartoon description was even available; both are dense_high_card_low (dense .991/.773 vs card .474/.234), consistent with the dense model rewarding standalone verbal craft that a visually-grounded scorecard cannot credit without an image referent.

proposals.name: Domestication of the fantastic into mundane routine
proposals.instruction: Score how fully the caption treats the cartoon's impossible or absurd element as an unremarkable, everyday occurrence, folding it into ordinary domestic/social logic with zero acknowledgment of its strangeness. 10 = the impossible premise is completely normalized into routine, low-stakes dialogue; 0 = the caption explicitly marks the scene as bizarre, shocking, or impossible.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') treats a shopping bear's checkout visit as an ordinary parenting-white-lie moment; R12 ('i'm thinking takeout') treats a booby-trapped kitchen as just another dinner-plan decision. Both dense_low_card_high (dense .338/.155 vs card .991/.975), the two highest card_pct scores in the slice.

proposals.name: Caption voiced from the anomalous/nonhuman character's POV
proposals.instruction: Score how clearly the caption is spoken in-character as the cartoon's impossible or anomalous figure (the animal, monster, or fantastical element) rather than by a neutral human bystander. 10 = caption is unambiguously voiced by the anomalous character with coherent internal logic from that perspective; 0 = caption is voiced by an unremarked outside observer commenting on the anomaly.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') is spoken as the shopping bear itself; R44 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big') is spoken as the wolf trying on the sheep costume; R28 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too') is voiced from inside the sheep/dog group. All three are dense_low_card_high (card .991/.822/.626), suggesting the scorecard rewards this perspective-taking device more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Implied unseen backstory beyond the depicted moment
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the caption gestures toward a specific prior event, history, or relationship dynamic that is not shown in the cartoon but that the reader must infer to get the joke. 10 = caption strongly implies a rich, specific unseen backstory (a betrayal, an escalating pattern, a hidden history); 0 = caption addresses only the visible instant with no implied history.
proposals.rationale: R48 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') implies an entire unseen backstory of deception/investigation; R60 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') implies an escalating, ongoing unseen history of dangerous dieting attempts. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .836/.656 vs card .338/.076).

proposals.name: Parodic institutional/statistical framing with invented figures
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption invents a specific number or formal phrase mimicking a real bureaucratic format (safety records, signage, official counts) to heighten deadpan realism. 10 = the caption clearly parodies a recognizable institutional format with an invented precise figure; 0 = no such statistical/institutional framing is used.
proposals.rationale: R50 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') parodies workplace safety-record signage; R53 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning') invents a precise incident count in an incident-log style. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .741/.880 vs card .195/.161).

proposals.name: Comic economy: punch lands with minimal, load-bearing words
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly compressed the caption is in achieving its comedic effect, with essentially no throat-clearing, hedging, or explanatory padding, ending on the load-bearing punch word. 10 = extremely compressed, every word necessary, caption ends on the punch; 0 = padded or explanatory phrasing dilutes or delays the punch.
proposals.rationale: R24 ('it's so ewe') delivers its full pun in four words with the punch as the final word; R33 ('you need to get your act together') is a short line that ends precisely on the double-meaning word 'act'. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .981/.991 vs card .159/.272), consistent with the dense model rewarding tight compression that a criterion-by-criterion scorecard may not specifically credit.

proposals.name: Terse fragment/staccato delivery
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption is delivered as short clipped fragments (very few words, punctuated as separate short bursts rather than one flowing sentence) rather than as a longer flowing sentence. 0 = long flowing single sentence with no internal breaks; 10 = extremely short, broken into staccato fragments/repeated short bursts. Score only the extent of this fragment/staccato quality present in the wording and punctuation; do not judge whether the caption is funny or good.
proposals.rationale: R15 ('six feet dude. six. feet', dense_pct=0.040/card_pct=0.953) and R43 ('honey, the remote is in your hand', dense_pct=0.225/card_pct=0.947) are terse/clipped and card-favored while dense ranks them low; a longer flowing line like R37 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent', dense_pct=0.859/card_pct=0.134) is dense-favored instead — brevity/rhythm is a stylistic tell, not per-cartoon fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (practiced entrant's clipped delivery rhythm)

proposals.name: Second-person direct address to a scene character
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption directly address 'you'/'your' to a character within or implied by the drawing (as opposed to using third person, first person only, or no addressee at all)? 0 = no second-person address anywhere in the caption; 10 = the caption is entirely built around directly addressing 'you'. Score only the presence/extent of this address form; do not judge whether the address is clever or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('...in your hand', card_pct=0.947) and R52 ('when you've mastered sit and stay you'll be a good boy too', card_pct=0.798) both build the line around direct 'you' address and are card-favored/dense-low, while a strong dense pick like R09 ('you're rambling again', dense_pct=0.991) also opens on 'you're' — the address form recurs across the slice independent of which model favors the item, marking it as a generic stylistic tell rather than fit.

proposals.name: Topical/political news reference
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption invoke a specific real-world contemporary political or news topic (e.g., named political parties, primaries, indictments, elections, votes, named institutions like 'white house') rather than staying entirely inside the invented scene of the cartoon? 0 = no real-world topical/political reference; 10 = the caption is built entirely around a specific real-world political/news reference. Score only the presence of such reference; do not judge whether the topical reference is well-executed or timely.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('republican primary ticket', dense_pct=0.751/card_pct=0.030), R04 ('he got indicted', dense_pct=0.957/card_pct=0.395), R19 ('it's the republican slate of candidates', dense_pct=0.764/card_pct=0.019), and R27 ('they're still looking for votes', dense_pct=0.970/card_pct=0.085) are all dense_high_card_low and all lean on a real-world political peg rather than the circus/detector scene itself — a timing-of-production tell, not a measure of fit to the drawing.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / news cycle at the moment of contest production

proposals.name: Hedging/self-qualifying discourse marker
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption contain hedging or self-qualifying discourse markers (e.g., 'actually', 'i think', 'i guess', 'in fact', 'well', 'you know') that comment on or soften the speaker's own statement, versus stating the line flatly with no such marker? 0 = no hedging marker present; 10 = the caption is built around one or more such qualifying markers. Score only the presence of the marker language; do not judge whether the hedge makes the joke better.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('...in fact, if you could toss it at me, that would be great', dense_pct=0.043/card_pct=0.569) and R48 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony', dense_pct=0.859/card_pct=0.353) both lean on this qualifying-speech pattern; it is a delivery habit a revision pass could introduce or remove regardless of how well the line fits its cartoon.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or revision practice applied before submission

proposals.name: Bare-pronoun opener assuming full context
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption open with a bare pronoun ('he', 'she', 'they', 'you're', 'it's') referring to a person or situation without any noun or scene-setting phrase to establish who or what is meant? 0 = caption opens with a concrete noun or scene-setting phrase; 10 = caption opens directly on an unexplained pronoun. Score only this opening-word pattern; do not judge whether the line is clear or confusing.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('you're rambling again', dense_pct=0.991/card_pct=0.474) and R27 ('they're still looking for votes', dense_pct=0.970/card_pct=0.085) both open on a bare pronoun and skip any restated scene detail, a habit of practiced entrants who trust the drawing to supply context rather than something diagnostic of fit to that specific cartoon.

proposals.name: Borrowed catchphrase or pre-existing cultural reference
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much of the caption's core wording is a direct quotation, near-quotation, or clearly recognizable paraphrase of a pre-existing song lyric, idiom, game-show format, or catchphrase that exists independently of this drawing? 0 = wording is original to this caption; 10 = the caption is essentially a restated well-known line or format. Score only how much borrowed/pre-existing phrasing is present; do not judge whether the borrowing is used cleverly.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('...never coming round the mountain', dense_pct=0.951/card_pct=0.444) and R08 ('...won't be comin' round the mountain', dense_pct=0.947/card_pct=0.191) both lean on the recognizable folk-song line, and R11 ('would you rather get back your truck, your dog, or your wife', dense_pct=0.405/card_pct=0.921) borrows the 'would you rather' game format — recognizability from outside the cartoon, not fit to it.

proposals.name: Obvious first-thought reading of the drawing
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption state the single most literal, first-thing-anyone-would-notice observation about the scene (the most obvious available pun or the most obvious mismatch/absurdity already named in the cartoon description) rather than an angle that requires a further inferential step? 0 = caption takes a distinctly non-obvious angle; 10 = the caption is the most generic, first-thought reading available for this scene. Score only how obvious/first-thought the reading is; do not judge whether that reading is well-written.
proposals.rationale: R30 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big', dense_pct=0.214/card_pct=0.822, wolf-in-sheep-costume cartoon) and R43 ('honey, the remote is in your hand', dense_pct=0.225/card_pct=0.947, metal-detector cartoon) each state the single most obvious, first-notice reading of their scene — the kind of angle many entrants for that same cartoon would independently reach, which is a position-in-the-entry-flood property, not evidence of fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: position among the flood of entries for its own cartoon

proposals.name: Uniform lowercase/no terminal punctuation transcription style
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how fully does the caption follow a flattened transcription style — entirely lowercase (no capital letters anywhere, including at the start of the sentence or for proper nouns) and no terminal punctuation mark (no period, question mark, or exclamation point at the very end)? 0 = caption uses standard capitalization and/or ends with punctuation; 10 = caption is fully lowercase throughout with no closing punctuation mark. Score only this transcription pattern; do not judge whether the styling is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Nearly the whole slice (e.g., R01 'he wasn't invited, but i left the light on'; R44 'i will give you no quarter') is rendered in this flattened all-lowercase, no-terminal-punctuation style, while a few entries deviate with internal periods or question marks (R15 'six feet dude. six. feet', R40 'oh, god. i think there's a theme'); this transcription convention is compiler-side, not caption-side quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: transcription/typography convention applied by whoever compiled the entry list

proposals.name: Risqué/off-color content register
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption contain sexual, off-color, or otherwise taboo/impolite content or innuendo, versus a fully family-friendly, decorous register? 0 = fully decorous, no off-color content; 10 = the caption is centrally built around risqué/taboo content. Score only the presence of such content; do not judge whether the risqué content is funny or tasteful.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('you should see the breasts', dense_pct=0.929/card_pct=0.042) and R37 ('...exposed skin implies consent', dense_pct=0.859/card_pct=0.134) are both dense_high_card_low with clearly off-color/risqué content, suggesting the scorecard's criterion bank systematically discounts this register independent of how well the line fits its cartoon.
proposals.upstream_parent: house style of the magazine running the contest (what register it prints)

proposals.name: Generic well-formed complete-sentence 'caption-shaped' joke
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption read as a fully-formed, grammatically complete, self-contained joke sentence with a clear setup-and-punchline shape that would be recognizable as 'a good caption' even to someone who has never seen this particular drawing, versus a fragment, an oblique aside, or a line that only makes sense once you already know the specific scene? 0 = incomprehensible or meaningless without the specific drawing; 10 = polished, complete, self-contained joke sentence that reads as generically caption-shaped. Score only this generic well-formedness; do not judge whether it is actually the best caption for this drawing.
proposals.rationale: R46 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon', dense_pct=0.338/card_pct=0.991) and R49 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish', dense_pct=0.452/card_pct=0.968) are both polished, complete, self-contained jokes that any generic reader would flag as 'a good caption,' and both are strongly card-favored while only dense-middling — showing generic well-formedness can be scored highly by a criterion bank without being what most distinguishes fit to this particular cartoon.

proposals.name: Withheld inferential step the reader must supply
proposals.instruction: Score how much unstated inference the reader must perform to connect the caption to the drawing. 10 = the caption never names the anomaly or the joke's hinge; it states something whose relevance only becomes clear once the reader completes a step the caption refuses to take (a hidden premise, an implied accusation, an unspoken identification). 5 = one small leap required. 0 = the caption spells out the connection completely, naming the odd element and its explanation, leaving the reader nothing to do. Judge only the size of the gap the reader must cross, not whether the joke is funny.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') never mentions metal detectors and forces the reader to reconstruct an entire accusation; R08 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony') likewise leaves the referent implicit. By contrast R09 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') and R32 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too') hand the reader the finished inference. A scorecard rewarding explicit, checkable linkage to cartoon elements will invert exactly this axis.

proposals.name: Redundant restatement of what is already visible
proposals.instruction: Score inversely for how much of the caption is spent describing content the drawing already shows. 10 = the caption adds entirely new information and describes nothing the viewer can see. 5 = it leans on one visible element as scaffolding but does work beyond it. 0 = the caption is essentially a verbal transcription of the picture (naming the visible resemblance, the visible object, the visible activity) with a joke tone applied on top. Restating is penalized even when the restatement is accurate and fluent.
proposals.rationale: R32 ('they think that we look alike too') restates the drawing's own stated oddity that the sheep and dogs look alike; R29 ('honey, the remote is in your hand') and R14 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') similarly narrate the visible situation. All three sit high on the scorecard and low on the dense model, which suggests the scorecard is crediting demonstrated engagement with the image while the dense model reads the same text as redundant.

proposals.name: Stock phrase or lyric literalized by the drawing, unnamed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption deploys an existing idiom, cliche, song lyric, or fixed expression whose literal reading is exactly what the drawing depicts, without flagging that it is doing so. 10 = a familiar phrase arrives in ordinary conversational use and the picture silently makes it literally true. 5 = a familiar phrase is used but only loosely fits the image, or the caption signals the borrowing. 0 = no stock phrase is in play, or a phrase is quoted with explicit acknowledgment that it is a reference.
proposals.rationale: R13 ('you need to get your act together') and R49 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') let a dead idiom come back to life against circus performers and a wool costume; R57 ('we have never had a cross word between us') and R17 ('discouraging words') and R33 ('she won't be comin' round the mountain') do the same with an idiom and with song lyrics. All are dense-high and scorecard-low, implying the bank does not detect phrase-level literalization.

proposals.name: Payload per word: extreme compression
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of comedic work done to words used. 10 = a very short caption (roughly one to six words, or a single coinage) that nonetheless carries the whole joke and could not be shortened. 5 = a normal-length line with no wasted words but no notable compression. 0 = a multi-clause caption in which several words or a whole clause could be deleted without losing anything. Length alone is not the criterion; a short caption that says little scores mid, not high.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('wreckmaninoff'), R23 ('it's so ewe'), R25 ('he got indicted') and R54 ('you're rambling again') are dense-high and card-low despite being extremely short, suggesting the scorecard undervalues or actively penalizes brevity. In the opposite direction R07 ('enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting') and R31 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make') are two-clause constructions scored high by the card and low by the dense model.

proposals.name: Implies an off-panel history between the characters
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption implies about the speakers' relationship and past beyond the single depicted moment. 10 = the line only makes sense if a whole prior history exists (a long marriage, a running deception, a family pattern), and the reader can feel that history without being told it. 5 = a mild relational hint. 0 = the caption is a self-contained remark that any stranger could make in that moment with no shared past.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') and R26 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') and R56 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning') each imply a long-running situation off the page and are all dense-high, card-low. R06 ('three more dollars and we can order a pizza') and R20 ('i'm thinking takeout') are relationally empty yet score high on the card.

proposals.name: Dark or transgressive content delivered deadpan
proposals.instruction: Score for content that is morbid, bodily, sexual, or ethically uncomfortable, delivered in a flat conversational register with no apology or wink. 10 = genuinely edgy material said as though it were small talk. 5 = mildly impolite. 0 = entirely wholesome content, or edgy content that is signposted, leering, or delivered with visible relish. Score the presence and deadpan handling of the transgression; do not penalize the caption for being impolite and do not reward mere shock without the flat delivery.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('you should see the breasts'), R18 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent'), R26 ('my dad lost a leg') and R30 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night') are all dense-high with very low card percentiles (0.042, 0.134, 0.076, 0.040), a pattern consistent with a bank that contains a tastefulness or appropriateness term suppressing exactly the material the dense model rewards.

proposals.name: Reframes the whole scene as public or institutional life
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption reinterprets the entire depicted absurdity as a comment on politics, institutions, or public life, rather than commenting on the scene's internal logic. 10 = a single phrase relabels every element of the drawing at once as something civic or institutional, and the mapping holds across the whole image. 5 = a passing political allusion attached to one element. 0 = no reframe of this kind.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('republican primary ticket'), R34 ('it's the republican slate of candidates') and R40 ('they're still looking for votes') and R50 ('our new white house collection') are all dense-high with card percentiles of 0.030, 0.019, 0.085 and 0.187. The scorecard appears to treat these as failing to engage with the drawing, while the dense model reads the relabeling as covering the whole image.

proposals.name: Perishable or already-expired topical reference
proposals.instruction: Score inversely for reliance on a reference tied to a specific recent news cycle whose salience has passed. 10 = the caption depends on nothing time-bound, or its topical reference is durable. 5 = a topical reference that still reads but dates the caption. 0 = the joke is entirely carried by a reference to a passing episode and collapses once that episode is no longer front of mind. Judge staleness from the reference itself, not from whether you find it funny.
proposals.rationale: R45 ('six feet dude. six. feet') and R03 ('remember when i was the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant') both lean wholly on pandemic-era framing and both sit very low on the dense model (0.040, 0.142) while scoring 0.953 and 0.781 on the card. A rubric that credits 'connects the image to a recognizable real-world situation' would over-reward precisely these.

proposals.name: Speaker choice is load-bearing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the joke depends on which figure in the drawing is speaking. 10 = the line is funny because this particular character says it, and reassigning it to another figure would destroy the joke. 5 = a plausible speaker exists but others would work about as well. 0 = the caption is speaker-indifferent; any character, or a narrator, could deliver it unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R44 and R51 ('no quarter') work only from the parent facing a coin-operated ride, and R18 ('exposed skin implies consent') works only from the mosquito; all three are dense-high and card-low. R06 ('three more dollars and we can order a pizza') and R20 ('i'm thinking takeout') are speaker-indifferent yet card-high, suggesting the bank checks that a speaker is plausible rather than that the speaker is necessary.

proposals.name: Pun anchored in vocabulary the scene already requires
proposals.instruction: Score whether wordplay is built from a word the scene forces into the sentence anyway, versus a word imported to enable the pun. 10 = the pivot word is one the speaker would naturally use in this situation, and its second meaning arrives as a bonus. 5 = the pun word fits but had to be steered toward. 0 = the sentence is visibly bent, or an unrelated object introduced, so the pun can happen.
proposals.rationale: R37 ('88 keys and no locks') and R23 ('it's so ewe') and R35 ('i love that it's 100 wool') use words the scene already demands (piano keys, sheep, wool) and are dense-high. R28 ('the only house i could find under a grand') and R05 ('that's a blues jay') import the pun and are dense-low despite card scores of 0.607 and 0.779, indicating the bank likely rewards pun presence without testing anchoring.

proposals.name: First-thought obviousness of the joke
proposals.instruction: Score inversely for predictability. Imagine a hundred people writing a caption for this drawing. 10 = almost none would arrive at this angle. 5 = a plausible but not inevitable angle. 0 = this is the single most obvious joke the drawing invites, the one a majority would write, executed competently. Competent execution of the obvious joke still scores 0 on this criterion.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish'), R14 ('my cubs still think i catch my own salmon'), R24 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big') and R05 ('blues jay') are the first jokes their drawings invite and all score card-high while the dense model puts them at 0.452, 0.338, 0.214 and 0.148. Fluency-and-relevance criteria cannot distinguish the obvious joke from the surprising one.

proposals.name: Flat register together with a second readable layer
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score high only when both hold: the caption is tonally flat, unbothered, and administratively ordinary, AND a second meaning is legible underneath that flatness. 10 = both fully present. 5 = flat delivery with only a thin second layer, or a good second layer delivered with visible effort or exclamation. 0 = flat with nothing underneath, or a second layer announced rather than buried.
proposals.rationale: R54 ('you're rambling again') and R25 ('he got indicted') and R12 ('of course we understand the gravity of our situation') pair total flatness with a live double meaning and are dense-high. R58 ('guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first') and R29 ('honey, the remote is in your hand') are equally flat but carry no second layer, yet score 0.767 and 0.947 on the card, so flatness alone is evidently being credited.

proposals.name: Introduces an outside fact that recontextualizes the frame
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption supplies a specific fact not visible in the drawing that changes how the drawing should be read. 10 = a concrete new datum (a number, a prior event, an absent third party) arrives and retroactively reorganizes the scene. 5 = a vague gesture outside the frame. 0 = the caption operates entirely within what is shown, adding no new fact.
proposals.rationale: R55 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') and R56 ('you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning') both introduce a specific count that reframes the image, and both are dense-high with card at 0.195 and 0.161. R58 and R32 stay strictly inside the frame and are card-high. A bank checking relevance to depicted elements would find outside facts less well supported.

proposals.name: Title-form captions judged on aptness, not dialogue plausibility
proposals.instruction: Score the aptness of the caption's chosen form. 10 = the caption is either natural in-world speech, or a deliberate label/title/coinage whose non-dialogue form is itself the point and which relabels the image precisely. 5 = form and content are mismatched but the line still functions. 0 = the form actively fights the content, for example a stilted line that is neither utterable speech nor a working title. Do not deduct for a caption being a label rather than a spoken line; deduct only for a label that does not land as a relabeling.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('republican primary ticket'), R34 ('it's the republican slate of candidates') and R43 ('wreckmaninoff') are non-dialogue labels with the lowest card percentiles in the slice (0.030, 0.019, 0.164) but dense percentiles of 0.751, 0.764 and 0.794. This is the signature of a bank criterion requiring plausible spoken dialogue, which penalizes a legitimate caption form outright.

proposals.name: Setup-then-explanation dilution
proposals.instruction: Score inversely for captions that make the joke and then account for it. 10 = one movement; the caption stops the instant the joke lands. 5 = a brief tag that does not explain. 0 = a clear two-part structure in which the second part justifies, elaborates, or supplies the reasoning behind the first, or a concessive opener ('on the plus side', 'believe it or not', 'actually') that pre-announces the joke's shape.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('on the plus side, mass extinction is a really cool band name'), R31 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make'), R09 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') and R59 ('eat it raw? what are we, neanderthals') all state and then justify, and all are card-high (0.516-0.847) while the dense model puts them at 0.021, 0.028, 0.006 and 0.106. Explanatory clauses plausibly read to a rubric as clarity and completeness.

proposals.name: Length, clause count and explanatory elaboration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how LONG and syntactically ELABORATED the caption is, counting only visible form. 0 = a bare fragment or single short phrase of roughly one to four words with no internal punctuation; 5 = one complete clause of roughly eight to twelve words; 10 = two or more clauses, or a sentence carrying a subordinate clause, a contrastive connective (but, given that, although, on the plus side), an internal comma or question mark, or a stated premise followed by a payoff. Count words and clause boundaries; add weight for internal punctuation that splits the line into set-up and follow-through. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the elaboration helps or hurts, or whether the caption is funny; report only how much elaboration is present.
proposals.rationale: Raw extent of text is a pure surface quantity yet it varies almost systematically across this slice, so any model reading raw text can key on it without keying on fit-to-cartoon. Terse fragments: R41 (it is so ewe), R56 (wreckmaninoff), R47 (he got indicted), R11 (you are rambling again). Elaborated multi-clause lines: R52 (enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting), R60 (i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover), R32 (are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make), R59. Length is not aboutness: R56 is one invented word and R60 is a full contrastive sentence, and neither word count tells you whether the line fits its drawing.

proposals.name: Homophone and lexicon-pun density on the depicted domain
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the caption consists of WORDPLAY built out of the vocabulary of the objects or animals named in the accompanying cartoon description: homophones and near-homophones (ewe/you, cross word/crossword, wool, keys, quarter), portmanteaus and name-blends, and idioms whose literal words are drawn from that same domain (pull the wool over my eyes, no quarter, herd immunity, get your act together). 0 = no sound-play or domain-idiom repurposing at all, the line is plain speech; 5 = one incidental domain word used idiomatically; 10 = the whole caption is the pun, with nothing left if the pun is removed. Count the mechanism, not the wit. You must NOT judge whether the pun is clever, groan-worthy, apt or original; report only how much of the line is pun machinery.
proposals.rationale: Pun density is mechanically detectable from lexical overlap between the caption and the cartoon description plus a homophone table, so a text model can score it without perceiving whether the joke lands. It varies enormously here: R41 (it's so ewe), R57 (pull the wool over my eyes), R50 (100 wool), R55 (88 keys and no locks), R56 (wreckmaninoff), R03 (cross word), R24 (gravity), R44 (pooped), R34 (blues jay), R17 (herd immunity) are near-pure pun, while R14 (honey, the remote is in your hand), R38 (guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first) and R52 contain none. Two captions can be equally strong or equally weak entries at either extreme, so the presence of the mechanism is a channel, not a quality.

proposals.name: Live-news political reference (news-cycle fingerprint)
proposals.instruction: MODE 2 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption depends on a REFERENCE TO CURRENT-EVENTS POLITICS or public-affairs news: named or implied parties, primaries, slates, tickets, candidates, votes and ballots, indictments, the White House, officeholders, campaigns, scandals. 0 = no political or civic content whatever; 3 = one glancing civic word that is not load-bearing; 7 = the joke's second meaning requires the reader to hold a political story in mind; 10 = the caption is nothing but the political reference. Judge only whether the political frame is present and how load-bearing it is.
