You must NOT judge whether the politics is timely, accurate, agreeable, tired or funny, and you must not form any view of the caption's merit.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2(a): an unobservable upstream factor here is WHICH WEEK the contest ran and what was dominating the news then; MODE 2(b): its textual fingerprint is exactly this vocabulary. The slice is loaded with it and it clusters: R08 (republican primary ticket) and R15 (it's the republican slate of candidates) are the same reference twice for the same drawing, plus R47 (he got indicted), R48 (they're still looking for votes), R09 (our new white house collection). A political reference is a fact about the calendar, not about how well the line reads the drawing, and a text-only model can pick up the vocabulary while learning nothing about fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: the news cycle live in the week the contest ran, and the entrant's news consumption

proposals.name: Datable era idiom fixing the entry to a period
proposals.instruction: MODE 3 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how strongly the caption's wording DATES it to a specific stretch of years, independent of any political content. Look for: pandemic-era idiom (distancing measures such as six feet, herd immunity, closures and shutdowns of restaurants or venues, masking, remote work); named consumer technology and platforms of a given moment (iphone, streaming, apps, texting); slang and address terms whose currency rises and falls (dude, hysterical); and conversely idiom that reads as older-register (telegram, party line). 0 = wording that would read the same in any decade; 5 = one mildly period-flavoured word; 10 = the caption cannot be understood without knowing what was happening in one particular year or two. You must NOT judge whether the dated reference is stale, fresh, or well used; score only how tightly the wording pins a period.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3: the actual contest date is invisible, but era leaves a lexical trace. Sharp examples inside the slice: R54 (six feet dude. six. feet), R17 (they claim they have herd immunity), R12 (the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant) all carry pandemic-window idiom; R06 (no tv or iphone) pins a consumer-technology era. Era membership is a property of when the entry was written, not of how well it reads its cartoon, yet it is highly visible in the tokens and therefore learnable by any text model as a shortcut.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the contest in the multi-year series (its era of conventions and shared references)

proposals.name: Crowd-obvious first-thought reading of the drawing
proposals.instruction: MODE 3 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption reads as the SINGLE MOST AVAILABLE angle on its cartoon, the line many independent entrants staring at that drawing would converge on. Indicators: it takes the most salient labelled object in the description and applies its most common idiom or homophone; it states the drawing's central incongruity in the plainest available words; the joke can be predicted from the description alone before reading the caption. 0 = an angle that requires a detail or association almost nobody would reach for; 5 = a moderately available angle; 10 = the first thing anyone would write. You must NOT judge whether the obvious reading is executed well or badly, and you must not treat obviousness as either a virtue or a fault; report availability only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3: entry-stream position is unobservable, but convergence is visible because the slice itself contains near-duplicates written for the same drawings. R36 (she's never coming round the mountain) and R42 (she won't be comin' round the mountain) are one angle twice; R21 (no. no quarter will be given) and R40 (i will give you no quarter) are one angle twice; R08 and R15 are one political angle twice; R23 (no bag. in fact, if you could toss it at me) and R59 (no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon) both open on the same no-bag move. Convergence indexes how crowded an angle is, which is a property of the entrant field rather than of the caption's fit, so it must not enter the criterion bank.
proposals.upstream_parent: the caption's position in the flood of entries submitted for its own cartoon

proposals.name: Caption narrates or explains the drawing rather than speaking inside it
proposals.instruction: MODE 2 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption RESTATES OR EXPLAINS what the cartoon description already says, instead of being a line a character would plausibly say in the moment. High scores for: naming the visible incongruity outright, telling the reader what to notice, glossing the situation, or supplying a caption that would be unintelligible if the reader could not see the drawing being described back to them. Low scores for: in-scene speech that presupposes the situation without describing it. 0 = pure in-scene utterance that never mentions what is visible; 10 = a sentence whose main content is a description of the picture. You must NOT judge whether explaining is a weakness or whether the line is funny; measure only the amount of drawing-restatement present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2(a) the unseen factor is how much the writer has internalised the form; MODE 2(b) its trace is the refusal-to-explain discipline. Visible contrast in the slice: R19 (believe it or not, they think that we look alike too) hands back the description's own observation that the sheep and dogs look alike, and R07 (when you've mastered sit and stay you'll be a good boy too) spells out the dog-behaving-as-human premise, whereas R33 (where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent) and R11 (you're rambling again) are flat in-scene speech that explains nothing. Tagged mixed because a practised entrant plausibly also writes genuinely better entries, so this parent is not purely nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the entrant's practice in this format (serial, rehearsed entrant versus one-off submitter)

proposals.name: Transcription and typography conventions of the compiled list
proposals.instruction: MODE 4 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much NON-DEFAULT TYPOGRAPHY the caption carries relative to the plain lowercase unpunctuated norm of this list. Add extent for: terminal punctuation present (a final period, question mark or exclamation); internal sentence-final periods splitting the line; quotation marks around an embedded phrase; double-hyphen or dash constructions; ellipses; digits written as numerals; symbols that appear stripped or mangled (a percentage or currency sign missing beside a number); any capitalisation at all. 0 = all lowercase, no terminal punctuation, no marks beyond a single comma; 10 = several of these conventions at once. You must NOT judge whether the punctuation is correct, careful or sloppy; count only how much marked typography is visible.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4: whoever compiled and normalised these entries left an uneven trace, and the unevenness is legible. R58 carries both quotation marks and a terminal period ('good girl.'), R59 uses a double hyphen (no bag--my cubs), R50 reads 100 wool with the percentage sign evidently lost in transcription, R28 carries a bare numeral (581 days), R54 uses sentence-final periods for emphasis (six. feet), while the great majority of rows such as R41, R11 and R14 are bare lowercase with no terminal mark. None of this is a property of the joke's fit to the drawing, but it is trivially learnable from raw text.
proposals.upstream_parent: the transcription and compilation pipeline that produced the entry list, plus the submitter's own typing habits

proposals.name: Generational reference register of the allusions used
proposals.instruction: MODE 2 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how far the caption's cultural allusions sit toward the OLDER, mid-century-canon end of the register rather than the contemporary end. High end: folk and standard songs, classical composers, classic detective fiction and its stock phrases, nautical or military archaisms, textbook prehistory, sayings of the when-I-was-a-kid form. Low end: contemporary devices, platforms, workplace idiom, current slang. Score 0 when the caption uses no cultural allusion whatever, 5 when allusions are era-neutral, 10 when the line is unintelligible to a reader who does not know a pre-1980 song, book, composer or catchphrase. You must NOT judge whether the allusion is charming, dated, apt or well chosen; place the register only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2(a) an unseen upstream factor is who submits to a long-running print caption contest and what canon they carry; MODE 2(b) its fingerprint is the allusion pool. Old-canon rows: R36 and R42 (she'll be comin' round the mountain), R25 (discouraging words, from Home on the Range), R56 (wreckmaninoff), R03 (my dear watson), R21 and R40 (no quarter), R46 (when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish). Contemporary-register rows: R06 (no tv or iphone), R47 (he got indicted), R54 (six feet dude). Cohort is not caption-cartoon fit, and it is fully visible in the lexicon, which makes it exactly the kind of shortcut a raw-text model can absorb.
proposals.upstream_parent: the entrant's demographic cohort and reading habits (age, cultural formation)

proposals.name: Off-colour or transgressive content against the venue register
proposals.instruction: MODE 4 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption reaches for TRANSGRESSIVE material relative to a restrained print register: sexual or anatomical innuendo, scatological humour, references to bodily functions, consent or assault framing, cruelty or graphic bodily harm, and shock reversals played straight. 0 = nothing a general-audience print venue would blink at; 5 = mild suggestion available only on a second reading; 10 = the caption's whole payload is the taboo element. You must NOT judge whether the transgression is funny, tasteless, brave or unprintable, and you must not consider whether an editor would run it; report only how much taboo content is present in the words.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4: house style is an unseen filter, and its complement is a visible textual property. The slice contains a clear transgressive cluster: R27 (you should see the breasts), R33 (exposed skin implies consent), R44 (we'll be pooped by the end of the night), R39 (my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg), against wholly tame rows such as R16 (i'm thinking takeout), R14 (honey, the remote is in your hand) and R38. Whether a line is racy is orthogonal to whether it reads its drawing well, so it must be discounted rather than credited.
proposals.upstream_parent: the house style and editorial register of the magazine running the contest

proposals.name: Generic well-formed caption-shaped correctness
proposals.instruction: MODE 5 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption matches the GENERIC TEMPLATE of a competent caption that any careful writer, or a general-purpose language model with no knowledge of this contest, would nominate: grammatical complete sentence; a conversational opener or discourse marker (i don't know about you but, actually, no, believe it or not, guess i'll, remember when); an explicit set-up followed by a tidy resolving payoff; the premise of the drawing acknowledged and then domesticated into an ordinary household or workplace complaint; nothing risky, ambiguous or unresolved left on the page. 0 = an odd, elliptical or unresolved line that does not fit the template at all; 10 = a textbook-shaped, smoothly finished, safely resolved caption. You must NOT judge whether such a caption is good, and in particular must not reward smoothness; measure only how closely the line matches the generic template.
proposals.rationale: MODE 5: several rows are exactly the safe, well-formed, obviously correct line, distinguishable purely by shape: R16 (i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout), R14 (honey, the remote is in your hand), R52 (enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting), R60 (i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover), R32 (are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make), R46 (when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish). Against them sit unsmoothed lines such as R11 (you're rambling again), R47 (he got indicted) and R56 (wreckmaninoff). Template-conformity is a prior over caption shape, not evidence about fit to a particular drawing. Tagged mixed because basic well-formedness plausibly also tracks real writing craft, so this channel belongs in the sensitivity band rather than being discounted outright.
proposals.upstream_parent: the generic competent-writer / general-purpose language-model prior over what a caption should look like

proposals.name: Multi-detail visual anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption jointly uses at least two concrete depicted details in one coherent joke; score 0 when it could fit without referring to the specific scene.
proposals.rationale: R01 combines the beam, gravity, and Grim Reaper; R06 combines the piano, house, keys, and locks; R27 turns the detectors into evidence about an engagement ring.

proposals.name: Semantic double-duty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a key word or phrase works literally for the image and simultaneously carries a distinct idiomatic or conceptual meaning; score 0 when it has only one reading.
proposals.rationale: R18 uses “crossword” and “cross word” alongside Watson; R22 turns a composer’s name into a wrecking-piano pun; R40 gives “herd immunity” both flock and public-health meanings.

proposals.name: Exact wordplay fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sound, spelling, or word substitution is precise, immediately recoverable, and tightly tied to the cartoon; score 0 when the wordplay is approximate or strained.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R07 exploit “quarter” precisely in the coin-operated ride; R58 makes “ewe” an exact sheep-related sound substitution.

proposals.name: Adapted familiar phrase
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable idiom, lyric, or saying is minimally altered so that its new wording fits the depicted situation; score 0 when a familiar phrase is merely pasted onto the scene.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R11 adapt “coming round the mountain”; R45 transforms “pull the wool over my eyes” for the wolf costume.

proposals.name: Structured cultural allusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an outside cultural or political reference maps meaningfully onto multiple visible elements or the scene’s central action; score 0 when it is only a topical name-drop.
proposals.rationale: R34 and R48 map a political slate or ticket onto the circus parade; R37 maps the six-day creation story onto the Earth piñata.

proposals.name: Deadpan tonal control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption’s matter-of-fact tone naturally treats the absurd scene as ordinary, thereby intensifying the contrast; score 0 when it overexplains, panics without purpose, or uses a mismatched tone.
proposals.rationale: R01 treats the Grim Reaper’s lunch as routine; R23 treats a living-room circus as background noise; R53 uses calm workplace language inside a creature-like tunnel.

proposals.name: Distinctive speaker viewpoint
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line clearly sounds like it comes from a particular depicted character and reveals that character’s situation or attitude; score 0 when no speaker perspective is implied or the line could be said by anyone.
proposals.rationale: R42 gives the mosquito a recognizable dispute about consent; R54 gives workers a specific accident-reporting perspective; R43 gives the sheep or dogs a situation-specific count.

proposals.name: Implied backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption makes a plausible unseen event, motive, or relationship inferable from the image; score 0 when it merely labels what is already visible.
proposals.rationale: R16 implies the kitchen’s defenses make cooking impractical; R21 suggests a family dispute over protected ice cream; R27 implies a missing engagement ring and relationship history.

proposals.name: Physical-gag exploitation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption turns the cartoon’s impossible scale, placement, or physics into a specific consequence or interpretation; score 0 when it ignores the physical contradiction.
proposals.rationale: R06 turns the giant piano into a house with keys and no locks; R33 uses the piano’s size in “under a grand”; R35 exploits the oversized meat’s anatomy.

proposals.name: Diagnostic-detail selection
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption selects the single most distinctive visual detail and builds a focused joke around it; score 0 when it uses a generic feature while overlooking what makes this cartoon unique.
proposals.rationale: R29 and R58 focus on the wolf’s wool costume; R41 focuses specifically on the wolf’s conspicuous teeth rather than generic animal behavior.

proposals.name: Beyond-premise surprise
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption adds an unexpected second interpretation rather than simply restating the cartoon’s absurd premise; score 0 when it supplies the obvious description or reaction.
proposals.rationale: R09 mainly restates that a bear catches fish; R30 simply explains why metal detectors are present; R57 largely repeats a pet-policy premise.

proposals.name: Scene-specific nonportability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke depends on this cartoon’s particular objects, relationships, or arrangement and would fail in most other cartoons; score 0 when it is a reusable stock remark.
proposals.rationale: R17’s distancing remark and R31’s pizza-money line are broadly portable; R50’s accountant comment and R52’s dog-training line likewise need little from their specific images.

proposals.name: Action-response coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption is a natural, causally intelligible response to what characters are doing or facing; score 0 when the wording is only loosely associated with the subject.
proposals.rationale: R16’s takeout suggestion directly follows from an unusable kitchen; R25’s request about the fish bag follows the bear’s handling needs; R46’s dessert remark addresses the Reaper’s presence at lunch.

proposals.name: Comedic turn clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording has a clear setup-to-payoff turn that an independent reader can identify immediately; score 0 when it remains a vague association, unfinished setup, or obscure reference.
proposals.rationale: R04’s light-on explanation and R24’s “host” pun provide surface associations without a strong turn; R59’s Saturn ring-toss line similarly shifts planets without clearly resolving the scene.

proposals.name: Authored conversational economy

proposals.rationale: R26 ('herd immunity' layers a sheep-herd pun, pandemic-era reference, and stubborn character voice) and R58 ('gravity' layers physical height, mortality, and pun on grave/serious) earn high dense scores through layering, while many dense_low items such as R20 and R60 operate on a single level the scorecard may find sufficient.

proposals.name: Register Incongruity
proposals.instruction: Score how comically wrong the caption's vocabulary, tone, or formality is for the depicted scenario. A 10 means the caption sounds like it belongs in a completely different context — a legal brief, medical chart, or HR meeting — applied to the drawing. A 0 means the caption uses natural conversational register appropriate to the scene.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('he got indicted' deploys legal language for a circus parade) and R47 ('exposed skin implies consent' applies philosophical/legal register to a mosquito) show the dense model rewarding register clashes the scorecard likely reads as tonal disconnect or irrelevance.

proposals.name: Punchline Unpredictability
proposals.instruction: Score how surprising the caption's meaning or ending is given the visual setup. A 10 means the caption arrives at a destination no reasonable person would predict from the drawing, yet it makes perfect sense in hindsight. A 0 means the punchline is the most obvious or expected first-thought response.
proposals.rationale: R01 (indictment for a circus — utterly unexpected) and R43 ('lost a leg' — the escalation from '45 pounds' is shocking) show the dense model crediting surprise, while dense_low items like R07 ('we had to catch our own fish') and R17 ('eat my dessert first') are highly predictable responses the scorecard may over-credit for straightforward relevance.

proposals.name: Pathos Beneath Absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score how much genuine emotional weight — sadness, regret, disappointment, vulnerability — the caption layers beneath the visual comedy. A 10 means the caption transforms a silly drawing into something unexpectedly moving or melancholic. A 0 means the caption is purely comedic with no emotional undercurrent.
proposals.rationale: R55 ('there never was an engagement ring' reveals heartbreak beneath a metal-detector search) and R43 (family tragedy beneath a kitchen gag) show the dense model crediting emotional depth that a checklist scorecard focused on cleverness or relevance likely overlooks.

proposals.name: Contemporary Cultural Anchor
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the caption ties the absurd visual to a recognizable contemporary trend, event, or shared cultural moment. A 10 means the caption instantly evokes a specific, timely context that sharpens the joke. A 0 means the caption is timeless or lacks any cultural reference point.
proposals.rationale: R26 ('herd immunity' — pandemic-era language applied to a sheep herd) and R35/R45 (political primary season applied to a circus) show the dense model valuing cultural timeliness, while the scorecard may treat topical resonance as a disconnect from the literal drawing.

proposals.name: Consequence Chain Implication
proposals.instruction: Score how vividly the caption implies a timeline of prior events and future fallout extending beyond the frozen moment of the drawing. A 10 means the caption makes the reader picture a full sequence of cause-and-effect, before and after. A 0 means the caption exists only in the present moment with no implied temporal extension.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('581 days without an accident' implies an entire safety record about to shatter) and R43 ('mom lost 45 pounds and dad lost a leg' implies repeated trap casualties over time) show the dense model crediting captions that crack the single-frame open into narrative time, a quality the scorecard may not measure.

proposals.name: Subject Deflection from Obvious
proposals.instruction: Score how far the caption pivots away from the drawing's most conspicuous element toward an oblique angle the reader must bridge. A 10 means the caption appears to address something entirely unrelated until the hidden connection clicks. A 0 means the caption directly names or addresses the single most obvious feature of the drawing.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('he got indicted' ignores the circus to comment on one person's stillness) and R47 ('exposed skin implies consent' ignores the mosquito to debate social philosophy) show the dense model rewarding oblique angles, while dense_low items like R20 ('the remote is in your hand') and R32 ('you ate dad's ice cream') address the drawing's most obvious feature directly — the scorecard may over-credit this directness as 'relevance.'

proposals.name: Obvious Idiom Taken Literally
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption's primary joke mechanism is applying a common idiom or cliché literally to the visual elements of the drawing (e.g., 'cross word', 'pull the wool'). The judge must not judge whether the feature is good.
proposals.rationale: Idioms are the easiest, most generic prior for a cartoon. Entries like R58 ('never had a cross word') and R17 ('pull the wool over my eyes') rely on this structural shortcut. A text-only model may score these highly because they perfectly map text to the image, but editors often reject them as uncreative first-thoughts.

proposals.name: Era-Specific Topical Reference
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption references a very specific contemporary news event, technology, or social phenomenon that firmly dates it to a particular week or brief era (e.g., covid distancing, recent elections). The judge must not judge whether this makes the caption good.
proposals.rationale: Entries such as R02 ('republican slate'), R35 ('herd immunity'), and R44 ('six feet dude') rely heavily on the news cycle of their specific contest week. A model might predict high engagement based on familiarity with the reference, but this is a temporal artifact rather than timeless caption quality.

proposals.name: Lowercase Transcription Typography
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption is written entirely in lowercase letters with no terminal punctuation (no periods, question marks, or exclamation points). The judge must not judge whether this formatting is good.
proposals.rationale: Many entries like R01 and R11 lack standard capitalization or punctuation entirely. This likely reflects the submission interface's quirks or the compilation process. It is a surface-level formatting artifact that visually distinguishes items but has no bearing on the actual humor.

proposals.name: Crude or Edgy Internet Humor
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption relies on scatological, dark, or edgy themes that feel borrowed from internet meme culture rather than traditional print cartoons. The judge must not judge whether the edginess is good.
proposals.rationale: Entries such as R13 ('you should see the breasts') and R38 ('exposed skin implies consent') use a tone typical of modern internet humor. A model might associate this transgressiveness with high engagement or distinctiveness, but it departs widely from the magazine's traditional house style.

proposals.name: Conversational Verbosity and Padding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption is padded with filler dialogue, unnecessary conversational throat-clearing, or unnatural spoken context (e.g., 'I don't know about you, but...', 'Enough about me...'). The judge must not judge whether the verbosity is good.
proposals.rationale: Practiced entrants tend to be punchy, while one-off submitters often over-explain the premise. Entries like R31 ('i don't know about you, but...') and R43 ('enough about me. you're an accountant?...') contain conversational padding. Verbosity is a strong textual fingerprint of an unpracticed author, which plausibly correlates with lower quality.

proposals.name: Corporate or Legal Jargon
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption uses modern corporate, legal, bureaucratic, or tech-support jargon (e.g., HR terms, business frameworks) to explain the cartoon's situation. The judge must not judge whether the jargon is good.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R03 ('it's not a grill problem it's a chicken problem') and R38 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent') map workplace or legal frameworks onto the cartoon. This is a fingerprint of the author's day job bleeding into the joke, which a model might score highly due to clever structural parallels.

proposals.name: Unanchored or Abstract Speaker
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption's spoken voice could be said by anyone and feels unanchored from the specific physical setting or characters depicted in the drawing. The judge must not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R19 ('you're rambling again') and R37 ('all my evaluation said was good girl') lack grounding in the specific visual elements. A dense model might score these highly because they are amusing in isolation, but a true contest entry must integrate tightly with its specific cartoon.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's cognitive style (writing a standalone tweet vs. a caption)

proposals.name: Celebrity Name Portmanteau
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the punchline is a simple pun, portmanteau, or homophone based on a famous historical or celebrity name. The judge must not judge whether the pun is good.
proposals.rationale: R18 ('wreckmaninoff') and R09 ('blues jay') rely on simple name wordplay. This surface pattern is structurally very easy for a language model to detect and generate as a 'pun,' but it represents a low-effort, easily substitutable form of wordplay rather than deep situational humor.

proposals.name: Domestic Relationship Drama
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption interprets the cartoon's events as a metaphor for standard romantic, marital, or domestic disputes. The judge must not judge whether this interpretation is good.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R07 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') and R42 ('i see you ate some of dad's favorite ice cream') project generic family drama onto absurd visuals. This is a highly recognizable generic prior for single-panel cartoons, which can be genuinely funny but is heavily overused.

proposals.name: Direct Real-World Labeling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption explicitly names or directly labels the literal objects, animals, or unusual elements in the drawing as its primary comedic mechanism. The judge must not judge whether the labeling is good.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R02 ('republican slate') and R60 ('white house collection') use direct political or real-world labeling to explain the drawing. This surface pattern relies merely on naming the real-world equivalent of the visual elements, a low-effort first-thought shortcut rather than an actual contest-worthy joke.

proposals.name: Metaphorical or Satirical Mapping
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption brilliantly maps the surreal visual elements to a recognizable real-world concept (e.g., a political process, social dysfunction, or bureaucracy) without over-explaining the connection; score 0 if the caption is entirely literal or misses the chance for metaphor.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly ranks captions that require the reader to bridge a visual absurdity to a real-world concept. Row R10 ('he got indicted') and R37 ('republican primary ticket') rank very high for the dense model but low for the scorecard, suggesting the scorecard misses these clever, cynical metaphorical mappings.

proposals.name: Maximum Punchline Economy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption achieves a massive conceptual twist using very few words (ideally 1-5 words), trusting the reader to fill in the blanks; score 0 if the caption is wordy, rambles, or over-explains the premise.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors extreme brevity that delivers a sharp twist. R17 ('it's so ewe') and R46 ('you're rambling again') are extremely short yet land a clever conceptual punch. The dense model rewards this efficiency, whereas the scorecard seems to favor more spelled-out setups.

proposals.name: Macabre or Edgy Subtext
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption confidently extracts a dark, morbid, or highly inappropriate implication from an otherwise mundane or silly visual; score 0 if the caption is sanitized, overly safe, or points out the obvious absurdity instead of the dark implication.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards captions that find the darkest or most transgressive angle of a drawing. R32 ('my dad lost a leg' regarding kitchen bear traps) and R47 ('exposed skin implies consent' regarding a mosquito) score high for the dense model but low for the scorecard, likely because the scorecard penalizes edgy humor.

proposals.name: Idiom or Phrase Literalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption takes a common idiom, saying, or phrase and makes it apply perfectly to the literal visual elements in the cartoon; score 0 if no common phrase is repurposed.
proposals.rationale: Applying idioms literally to surreal scenes is a strong indicator of contest-quality humor that requires deep semantic understanding. R40 ('no quarter will be given' for a coin-operated horse) and R49 ('i will give you no quarter') are loved by the dense model but missed by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Generative Implied Backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption completely reframes the drawing by introducing an unexpected hidden motive or past/future event that changes the context of the scene; score 0 if the caption merely describes what is obviously happening in the drawing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values captions that use the drawing as a jumping-off point for a larger narrative twist. R51 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') and R34 ('you need to get your act together') create a brilliant subtext that the scorecard fails to credit.

proposals.name: Multi-Layered Double Entendre
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption features a word or phrase that operates simultaneously on two distinct levels (e.g., a material property and a social/visual concept) that both perfectly fit the cartoon; score 0 if the caption's meaning is purely single-layer and literal.
proposals.rationale: The dense model excels at perceiving layers of meaning. R15 ('i love that it's 100 wool') and R26 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony') feature double meanings (material/pun, literal/metaphorical) that rank highly for the dense model, suggesting the scorecard misses these layered wordplays.

proposals.name: Avoidance of Heavy-Handed Explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption trusts the reader entirely, dropping a punchline without spelling out the premise or the joke; score 0 if the caption painfully spells out the joke, uses unnecessary dialogue tags, or points out the surreal element too directly.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard seems to over-credit captions that explicitly narrate the visual absurdity, which the dense model penalizes. R09 ('mass extinction is a really cool band name') and R59 ('eat it raw? what are we, neanderthals') are heavy-handed and explanatory, scoring low for the dense model but high for the scorecard.

proposals.name: Strict Fidelity to Drawn Elements
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption cleverly plays off a highly specific, obscure detail drawn in the cartoon; score 0 if the caption ignores the specific details of the drawing and relies on generic tropes or makes factually mismatched claims about the image.
proposals.rationale: The dense model evaluates the caption against the precise visual context, penalizing lazy factual mismatches. R45 ('it's a chicken problem' when the drawing says giant piece of meat) is dense_low_card_high, while R06 ('you should see the breasts') is dense_high_card_low for matching the meat. The scorecard misses these specific visual-text alignments.

proposals.name: Seamless Neologism or Portmanteau
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption invents a clever, seamless new word, pun, or portmanteau that perfectly encapsulates the visual disaster; score 0 if the caption relies entirely on standard, predictable vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: Creating a perfect neologism demonstrates high-level linguistic play that the dense model recognizes. R56 ('wreckmaninoff' for a piano crash) is heavily favored by the dense model over standard reactions, indicating the scorecard lacks a metric for rewarding creative word coinage.

proposals.name: Conversational Deadpan Delivery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption mimics a completely mundane, casual remark or complaint that sharply contrasts with the absolute chaos or surrealism of the drawing; score 0 if the tone is melodramatic, exclamatory, or explicitly acknowledges the weirdness.
proposals.rationale: The juxtaposition of a casual tone with a chaotic scene is a classic contest technique. R10 ('he got indicted') and R46 ('you're rambling again') rank incredibly high for the dense model because they treat the surreal parade with deadpan casualness, a nuance the scorecard appears to miss.

proposals.name: Interpersonal Conflict Pivot
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption turns a bizarre visual scenario into a commentary on a relatable interpersonal relationship or marital dispute; score 0 if it focuses entirely on the physical objects or the literal strange creature in the drawing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appreciates when a caption shifts focus from the weird visual to human relationship dynamics. R51 ('there never was an engagement ring') transforms a metal detector scene into a relationship tragedy. Conversely, R04 ('honey, the remote is in your hand') is too obvious, scoring low for dense.

proposals.name: Cynical or Legalistic Anthropomorphism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if an animal or inanimate object is given a highly specific, jaded, legalistic, or bureaucratic human motivation that perfectly clashes with its nature; score 0 if the animal is just given a generic, cute human trait.
proposals.rationale: Instead of basic anthropomorphism, the dense model rewards specific, cynical human traits. R47 ('exposed skin implies consent') and R60 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night') give jaded/human traits to a mosquito and digestive tract respectively, scoring highly for dense, while the scorecard undervalues this cynical layer.

proposals.name: Musical or Cultural Reference Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption integrates a song title, lyric, or classical cultural reference in a way that physically or contextually matches the visual disaster; score 0 if there is no cultural or musical reference.
proposals.rationale: Tying a specific song to the visual elements requires deep conceptual linking. R16 ('won't be comin' round the mountain') and R50 ('never coming round the mountain') rank very high for the dense model, suggesting the scorecard lacks a way to reward clever musical/cultural integration.

proposals.name: Lazy Anachronism Penalty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption avoids lazy historical or time-period jokes; score 0 if the caption relies entirely on the obvious time-period clash (e.g., cavemen acting like modern people, animals using modern technology) without adding a deeper twist.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard seems easily impressed by basic anachronism, whereas the dense model recognizes it as a lazy trope. R59 ('what are we, neanderthals') and R38 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish') score low for the dense model because they lean entirely on obvious time-period clashes.

proposals.name: Meta-Textual or Genre Awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption cleverly comments on the nature of the scene as if it were a puzzle, text, or specific genre trope (e.g., treating a crossword puzzle as a literal mystery); score 0 if the caption ignores the structural or meta-nature of the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors captions that playfully acknowledge the genre or structure of the scenario. R26 ('detect irony' instead of metal) and R25 ('cross word between us' for a crossword puzzle) show high-level meta-awareness that the dense model rewards heavily, but the scorecard misses.

proposals.name: Obvious first-thought pun
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption relies on the single most obvious wordplay or literal interpretation directly invited by the cartoon's main visual element (e.g., 'wool' for a wolf in sheep's clothing). Explicitly do not judge whether the pun is funny.
proposals.rationale: Captions like 'pull the wool over my eyes' (R32) or 'it's so ewe' (R03) are highly predictable consensus readings of the image that thousands of entrants would also write, representing the most crowded angle rather than a unique contest entry.

proposals.name: Topical news and era reference
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the caption explicitly references a specific contemporary political event, public figure, or cultural news item (e.g., elections, pandemics, indictments) that dates it to a particular week's news cycle. Do not judge the funniness of the reference.
proposals.rationale: References like 'he got indicted' (R26), 'republican primary ticket' (R11), and 'herd immunity' (R34) date the entry to a specific era, which models might key on for general relevance without reflecting timeless caption quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: the news cycle at the moment of the contest

proposals.name: Generic-prior guessable pun
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the caption reads like a standard, safe, well-formed pun or joke that any competent writer or general language model would immediately generate for the described scene. Explicitly do not judge whether the joke is actually good.
proposals.rationale: Captions like 'the gravity of our situation' (R43) for workers on a high beam are perfectly structured generic puns that a generic prior loves, but editors often find them cliché. Same for R49's 'cross word' pun.

proposals.name: Lowercase submission formatting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption is written entirely in lowercase letters without standard sentence capitalization. Do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: The overwhelming majority of entries, such as R01 and R14, are typed in all lowercase, a specific digital submission or compilation habit artifactually correlated with the dataset's presentation.

proposals.name: Staccato punctuation and typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption uses specific typography like dashes (e.g., '--') or abrupt periods for conversational pauses instead of standard commas. Do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R38 ('no bag--my cubs...') and R47 ('six feet dude. six. feet') use staccato punctuation, a specific typographical habit of the submitter that stands out structurally to models.

proposals.name: Meta-commentary on visual absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption explicitly points out or plays on the literal absurdity of the scene itself in a self-aware manner. Do not judge if it is funny.
proposals.rationale: Captions like 'you need to get your act together' (R41) for a circus parade, or noticing a 'theme' in a crossword puzzle (R25), point directly at the cartoon's premise rather than inventing a unique fictional world, a common amateur tactic.

proposals.name: Extreme brevity or fragment
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption is extremely short, consisting of a single word, a name, or a brief fragment lacking a full sentence structure. Do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R52 ('wreckmaninoff') and R14 ('you're rambling again') rely on extreme brevity, a hallmark of a practiced submission strategy aiming for deadpan delivery, which structurally influences scores.

proposals.name: Conversational over-explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption uses conversational filler, rhetorical questions, or multi-part sentence structures to over-explain the premise or set up the punchline. Do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Captions like R19 ('on the plus side, mass extinction is a really cool band name') or R06 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too') use verbose scaffolding to force the joke, a fingerprint of less disciplined writing.

proposals.name: Pun portmanteau or neologism
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption invents a single-word portmanteau, neologism, or surreal name as the entire punchline. Do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Entries like R52 ('wreckmaninoff') or R03 ('it's so ewe') rely on inventing a word or punny distortion, a highly specific style of wordplay that some models rate highly for surface-level cleverness.

proposals.name: Disconnected absurdist non-sequitur
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption offers an absurdist statement, non-sequitur, or surreal observation that barely connects to the specific details of the drawing but sounds generally witty. Do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Captions like R07 ('all my evaluation said was good girl') and R14 ('you're rambling again') are vague absurdist lines that represent a generic attempt at wry humor rather than a targeted contest entry.
